notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Biodiversity means the variety and variability of living organisms.
  • It includes diversity within species, between species and among ecosystems.
  • India has very high biological diversity because of its wide variation in climate, relief, soils and habitats.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biodiversity → Genetic + Species + Ecosystem Diversity

2. Three Levels of Biodiversity

The three major levels are:

  • Genetic diversity.
  • Species diversity.
  • Ecosystem diversity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Three Levels → Genetic + Species + Ecosystem

3. Genetic Diversity
  • Genetic diversity is variation in genes within a species.
  • It allows populations to adapt to environmental changes.
  • Traditional crop varieties and livestock breeds are examples of genetic diversity.
4. Species Diversity
  • Species diversity refers to the variety of different species within an area.
  • Tropical forests and coral reefs generally support high species diversity.
5. Ecosystem Diversity
  • Ecosystem diversity refers to the variety of habitats and ecological systems.
  • Indian examples include:
  • Himalayas.
  • Tropical forests.
  • Grasslands.
  • Deserts.
  • Wetlands.
  • Mangroves.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Islands.
6. India's Biodiversity

India contains:

  • Tropical ecosystems.
  • Temperate ecosystems.
  • Alpine ecosystems.
  • Desert ecosystems.
  • Freshwater systems.
  • Marine ecosystems.

This geographical diversity supports a very wide range of flora and fauna.

7. Causes of India's High Biodiversity

Important factors include:

  • Large latitudinal extent.
  • Great altitudinal variation.
  • Monsoon climate.
  • Long coastline.
  • Himalayan mountains.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Islands.
  • Major river systems.
8. Flora
  • Flora means plant life of a particular region.
  • It includes natural vegetation and plant species occurring in that area.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Flora → Plants

9. Fauna
  • Fauna means animal life of a particular region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fauna → Animals

10. Wildlife
  • Wildlife broadly refers to undomesticated plants and animals living in natural habitats.
  • In common exam usage, it often refers mainly to wild animals.
11. Habitat
  • Habitat is the natural place where an organism lives.
  • It provides:
  • Food.
  • Water.
  • Shelter.
  • Breeding space.
12. Niche
  • An ecological niche describes the functional role of a species in its ecosystem.
  • It includes how the species uses resources and interacts with other organisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Habitat → Where It Lives

Niche → How It Lives / Its Ecological Role

13. Endemic Species
  • An endemic species is naturally restricted to a particular geographical region.
  • Endemism is high in isolated or ecologically specialised regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Endemic → Restricted to a Particular Region

14. Examples of High-Endemism Regions in India

Important regions include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Eastern Himalayas.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Some northeastern hill systems.
15. Exotic Species
  • Exotic species are species introduced outside their natural geographical range.
  • They are also called alien or non-native species.
16. Invasive Alien Species
  • An invasive alien species is a non-native species that spreads rapidly and causes ecological or economic harm.
  • Not every exotic species becomes invasive.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Exotic ≠ Automatically Invasive

17. Important Invasive Plants in India

Examples include:

  • Lantana camara.
  • Prosopis juliflora.
  • Water hyacinth.
  • Parthenium hysterophorus.
18. Water Hyacinth
  • Water hyacinth is an invasive aquatic plant.
  • It can form dense mats over water bodies.
  • It reduces:
  • Light penetration.
  • Dissolved oxygen.
  • Navigation.
  • Native biodiversity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Hyacinth → Invasive Aquatic Plant

19. Parthenium
  • Parthenium hysterophorus is an invasive weed.
  • It spreads rapidly in disturbed land.
  • It can affect agriculture, native vegetation and human health.
20. Native Species
  • Native species occur naturally within a geographical region.
  • Native does not necessarily mean endemic.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Native ≠ Endemic

21. Threatened Species
  • Threatened species face a significant risk of extinction.
  • The term commonly includes categories such as:
  • Vulnerable.
  • Endangered.
  • Critically Endangered.
22. Extinction
  • Extinction occurs when no living individual of a species remains.
  • Extinction is irreversible.
23. Local Extinction
  • Local extinction occurs when a species disappears from one geographical area but survives elsewhere.
  • It is also called extirpation.
24. IUCN
  • IUCN stands for International Union for Conservation of Nature.
  • It is widely known for assessing the conservation status of species.
📌 Must-Memorise

IUCN → International Union for Conservation of Nature

25. IUCN Red List
  • The IUCN Red List assesses extinction risk of species.
  • Major categories include:
  • Extinct.
  • Extinct in the Wild.
  • Critically Endangered.
  • Endangered.
  • Vulnerable.
  • Near Threatened.
  • Least Concern.
  • Data Deficient.
26. Critically Endangered
  • Critically Endangered species face an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild.
27. Endangered
  • Endangered species face a very high risk of extinction in the wild.
28. Vulnerable
  • Vulnerable species face a high risk of extinction in the wild.
29. Data Deficient
  • Data Deficient means available information is insufficient to assess extinction risk accurately.
  • It does not mean the species is safe.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Data Deficient ≠ Least Concern

30. Biodiversity Hotspot
  • A biodiversity hotspot is a region with exceptionally high endemism and severe habitat loss.
  • Hotspot status is based on global conservation criteria.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hotspot → High Endemism + High Habitat Loss

31. Global Hotspots Covering Parts of India

Four globally recognised biodiversity hotspots include parts of India:

  • Himalaya.
  • Indo-Burma.
  • Western Ghats-Sri Lanka.
  • Sundaland.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → 4 Biodiversity Hotspots

32. Himalaya Hotspot
  • The Himalaya hotspot includes biologically rich Himalayan regions.
  • Elevation produces great habitat variation.
  • Eastern Himalayan sectors are especially species-rich.
33. Indo-Burma Hotspot
  • Indo-Burma includes much of northeastern India and adjoining Southeast Asian regions.
  • It contains rich forest and freshwater biodiversity.
34. Western Ghats-Sri Lanka Hotspot
  • Western Ghats are among India's most important biodiversity regions.
  • They contain many endemic:
  • Plants.
  • Amphibians.
  • Reptiles.
  • Freshwater fishes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Western Ghats → High Endemism

35. Sundaland Hotspot
  • In India, the Sundaland hotspot is represented by the Nicobar Islands.
  • The hotspot extends mainly across Southeast Asian island regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Part of Sundaland → Nicobar Islands

36. Western Ghats Biodiversity

Important features include:

  • Tropical evergreen forests.
  • Shola-grasslands.
  • Montane forests.
  • High amphibian endemism.
  • Rich plant diversity.
37. Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity
  • Eastern Himalayas receive heavy rainfall.
  • They contain tropical, subtropical, temperate and alpine habitats.
  • Species diversity is generally higher than in many drier western Himalayan regions.
38. Island Biodiversity

Islands often have high endemism because of geographical isolation.

Indian examples:

  • Andaman Islands.
  • Nicobar Islands.
  • Lakshadweep marine ecosystems.
39. Coral Reef Biodiversity
  • Coral reefs support very high marine biodiversity.
  • They provide:
  • Fish habitat.
  • Nursery grounds.
  • Coastal protection.
40. Major Coral Reef Regions of India

Important reef areas include:

  • Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Gulf of Mannar.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Coral Regions → Kachchh + Lakshadweep + Gulf of Mannar + A&N

41. Coral
  • Reef-building corals are marine animals living in colonies.
  • Many have a symbiotic relationship with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae.
42. Coral Bleaching
  • Coral bleaching occurs when corals lose or expel their symbiotic algae under stress.
  • High sea temperature is a major cause.
  • Prolonged bleaching can cause coral death.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coral Bleaching → Loss of Symbiotic Algae

43. Mangrove Biodiversity
  • Mangroves support:
  • Fish.
  • Crabs.
  • Molluscs.
  • Birds.
  • Reptiles.
  • They are important nursery habitats.
44. Wetland Biodiversity

Wetlands support:

  • Waterbirds.
  • Fish.
  • Amphibians.
  • Aquatic plants.
  • Invertebrates.

They also regulate floods and water quality.

45. Grassland Biodiversity
  • Grasslands support specialised wildlife.
  • They should not automatically be considered degraded forests.
  • Natural grasslands are distinct ecosystems.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Natural Grassland ≠ Wasteland

46. Desert Biodiversity
  • Deserts contain species adapted to heat, drought and scarce water.
  • Important Indian desert fauna include:
  • Chinkara.
  • Desert fox.
  • Great Indian Bustard.
  • Reptiles.
47. Alpine Biodiversity
  • Alpine ecosystems occur above the Himalayan tree line.
  • They contain:
  • Grasses.
  • Herbs.
  • Dwarf shrubs.
  • They support specialised mountain fauna.
48. Major Causes of Biodiversity Loss

Important causes include:

  • Habitat loss.
  • Habitat fragmentation.
  • Overexploitation.
  • Pollution.
  • Invasive species.
  • Climate change.
  • Poaching.
49. Habitat Loss
  • Habitat loss occurs when natural ecosystems are converted into:
  • Farms.
  • Roads.
  • Mines.
  • Settlements.
  • Industries.

It is one of the most important drivers of biodiversity decline.

50. Habitat Fragmentation
  • Fragmentation divides a large continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches.
  • It reduces wildlife movement and genetic exchange.
51. Edge Effect
  • Fragmentation creates more habitat edges.
  • Environmental conditions at edges differ from the interior.
  • This is called the edge effect.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Fragmentation → Edge Effect

52. Wildlife Corridor
  • A wildlife corridor connects separated habitat patches.
  • It allows:
  • Migration.
  • Seasonal movement.
  • Genetic exchange.
53. Elephant Corridors
  • Elephant corridors connect habitats used by elephant populations.
  • Blocking corridors can increase human-elephant conflict.
54. Overexploitation
  • Overexploitation occurs when species are harvested faster than they can reproduce.
  • It can affect:
  • Timber species.
  • Fish.
  • Medicinal plants.
  • Wildlife.
55. Poaching
  • Poaching is illegal hunting, capturing or killing of wildlife.
  • It threatens species targeted for:
  • Skin.
  • Horn.
  • Tusks.
  • Meat.
  • Traditional medicine.
  • Pet trade.
56. Illegal Wildlife Trade
  • Illegal trade affects many species.
  • It operates across national borders.
  • Strong enforcement and international cooperation are necessary.
57. Human-Wildlife Conflict

Human-wildlife conflict may involve:

  • Crop damage.
  • Livestock predation.
  • Property damage.
  • Human injury.
  • Wildlife mortality.
58. Causes of Human-Wildlife Conflict

Important causes include:

  • Habitat fragmentation.
  • Corridor blockage.
  • Agricultural expansion.
  • Roads.
  • Settlements near forests.
  • Food attractants.
59. In-Situ Conservation
  • In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats.

Examples include:

  • National parks.
  • Wildlife sanctuaries.
  • Biosphere reserves.
  • Conservation reserves.
  • Community reserves.
📌 Must-Memorise

In-Situ → Conservation in Natural Habitat

60. Ex-Situ Conservation
  • Ex-situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitats.

Examples include:

  • Zoos.
  • Botanical gardens.
  • Seed banks.
  • Gene banks.
  • Captive-breeding centres.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ex-Situ → Conservation Outside Natural Habitat

61. In-Situ vs Ex-Situ

In-situ:

  • Protects entire natural ecosystem.
  • Maintains ecological interactions.

Ex-situ:

  • Focuses on selected species or genetic material.
  • Useful for critically threatened populations.
62. National Park
  • A national park is a legally protected area established for conserving wildlife and ecosystems.
  • Human activities are highly restricted.
  • Rights and resource extraction are more strictly controlled than in many sanctuary settings.
63. Wildlife Sanctuary
  • A wildlife sanctuary protects wild animals and their habitats.
  • Certain regulated human activities or rights may continue depending on legal provisions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary → Not Identical

64. Biosphere Reserve
  • A biosphere reserve is a large landscape-level conservation area.
  • It combines:
  • Biodiversity conservation.
  • Sustainable use.
  • Research and monitoring.
65. Three Zones of Biosphere Reserve

A biosphere reserve generally contains:

  • Core zone.
  • Buffer zone.
  • Transition zone.
📌 Must-Memorise

Biosphere Reserve → Core + Buffer + Transition

66. Core Zone
  • Core zone receives the highest level of protection.
  • Conservation and research are primary functions.
67. Buffer Zone
  • Buffer zone surrounds or adjoins the core.
  • Limited research, education and compatible activities may occur.
68. Transition Zone
  • Transition zone allows settlements and sustainable economic activity.
  • It aims to demonstrate conservation-compatible development.
69. Conservation Reserve
  • Conservation reserves are protected areas generally declared on government land adjoining protected areas or linking habitats.
  • They are intended to conserve landscapes, seascapes and corridors.
70. Community Reserve
  • Community reserves involve conservation on community or private lands where local communities participate in protection.
71. Protected Area Network

India's protected-area system includes:

  • National parks.
  • Wildlife sanctuaries.
  • Conservation reserves.
  • Community reserves.

Exact totals change over time and should be taken from the latest official records when asked numerically.

72. Biosphere Reserve vs National Park

Biosphere Reserve:

  • Very large landscape.
  • Can contain settlements.
  • Has zonation.
  • May include national parks and sanctuaries.

National Park:

  • More strictly protected legal area.
  • Smaller and more focused on ecosystem/wildlife protection.
73. Marine Protected Areas
  • Marine protected areas conserve:
  • Coral reefs.
  • Seagrass.
  • Mangroves.
  • Marine animals.
  • India has several protected marine and coastal ecosystems.
74. Species Conservation Programmes

Major conservation programmes in India have focused on species such as:

  • Tiger.
  • Elephant.
  • Crocodile.
  • Rhinoceros.
  • Vultures.
  • Snow leopard.
75. Project Tiger
  • Project Tiger was launched in 1973.
  • It aims to conserve tigers and their habitats.
  • Tiger reserves operate through core and buffer landscape management.
📌 Must-Memorise

Project Tiger → 1973

76. Tiger as Umbrella Species
  • Protecting large tiger habitats also protects many other species living in the same ecosystem.
  • Such a species is often described as an umbrella species.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tiger → Umbrella Species Concept

77. Tiger Reserve
  • A tiger reserve is a designated landscape for tiger conservation.
  • It generally includes:
  • Core/critical tiger habitat.
  • Buffer/peripheral area.
78. Project Elephant
  • Project Elephant was launched in 1992.
  • It focuses on:
  • Elephant conservation.
  • Habitat protection.
  • Migration corridors.
  • Human-elephant conflict.
📌 Must-Memorise

Project Elephant → 1992

79. Elephant Landscape
  • Asian elephants require large connected habitats.
  • They move seasonally across forests, grasslands and agricultural landscapes.
80. One-Horned Rhinoceros
  • The greater one-horned rhinoceros is strongly associated with northeastern India.
  • Assam is its most important Indian stronghold.
81. Kaziranga National Park
  • Kaziranga lies in Assam.
  • It is famous for:
  • Greater one-horned rhinoceros.
  • Elephants.
  • Tigers.
  • Floodplain grasslands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kaziranga → Assam → One-Horned Rhinoceros

82. Manas
  • Manas lies in Assam near the Bhutan border.
  • It contains rich grassland and forest ecosystems.
  • It is associated with several rare mammals.
83. Gir National Park
  • Gir lies in Gujarat.
  • It is famous as the natural stronghold of the Asiatic lion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gir → Gujarat → Asiatic Lion

84. Asiatic Lion
  • The wild Asiatic lion population is strongly associated with Gujarat's Gir landscape.
85. Snow Leopard
  • Snow leopards inhabit high-altitude Himalayan and Trans-Himalayan regions.
  • They are adapted to cold, rugged mountain environments.
86. Hemis National Park
  • Hemis lies in Ladakh.
  • It is famous for snow leopard habitat.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hemis → Ladakh → Snow Leopard

87. Red Panda
  • Red panda occurs in the eastern Himalayas.
  • Indian habitats include parts of:
  • Sikkim.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Northern West Bengal.
88. Hangul
  • Hangul is the Kashmir stag.
  • It is associated with the Kashmir Valley region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hangul → Kashmir Stag

89. Dachigam National Park
  • Dachigam lies near Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir.
  • It is strongly associated with the conservation of Hangul.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dachigam → Hangul

90. Wild Ass
  • The Indian wild ass is strongly associated with the Little Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat.
91. Wild Ass Sanctuary
  • Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary lies in the Little Rann of Kachchh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Little Rann of Kachchh → Indian Wild Ass

92. Great Indian Bustard
  • Great Indian Bustard is associated with arid and semi-arid grasslands.
  • Rajasthan is one of its most important remaining landscapes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Great Indian Bustard → Rajasthan Grasslands

93. Keoladeo National Park
  • Keoladeo National Park lies at Bharatpur in Rajasthan.
  • It is famous for wetlands and waterbirds.
  • It was historically known as Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary.
📌 Must-Memorise

Keoladeo → Bharatpur → Rajasthan

94. Desert National Park
  • Desert National Park lies in Rajasthan.
  • It protects Thar Desert ecosystems.
  • Great Indian Bustard is an important species of this landscape.
95. Gharial
  • Gharial is a specialised fish-eating crocodilian.
  • It inhabits relatively clean river systems with sandy banks.
96. National Chambal Sanctuary
  • National Chambal Sanctuary protects riverine wildlife.
  • It is especially known for:
  • Gharial.
  • Gangetic dolphin.
  • River turtles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chambal → Gharial

97. Crocodilian Groups in India

Important crocodilians include:

  • Gharial.
  • Mugger crocodile.
  • Saltwater crocodile.
98. Saltwater Crocodile
  • Saltwater crocodiles occur in coastal and estuarine habitats.
  • Important populations occur in:
  • Odisha.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Sundarbans and adjoining regions.
99. Bhitarkanika
  • Bhitarkanika lies in Odisha.
  • It is famous for:
  • Mangroves.
  • Estuarine crocodiles.
  • Coastal biodiversity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhitarkanika → Odisha → Mangroves + Saltwater Crocodile

100. Gangetic Dolphin
  • Gangetic dolphin is a freshwater cetacean.
  • It inhabits parts of the Ganga-Brahmaputra river system.
  • It depends on deep river channels and adequate flow.
101. Dolphin as River-Health Indicator
  • River dolphins require functioning freshwater ecosystems.
  • Their decline can indicate habitat degradation and water pollution.
102. Olive Ridley Turtle
  • Olive Ridley sea turtles are famous for mass nesting along parts of Odisha's coast.
  • Mass nesting is called arribada.
📌 Must-Memorise

Olive Ridley → Odisha Coast → Arribada

103. Gahirmatha
  • Gahirmatha coast in Odisha is famous for Olive Ridley turtle nesting.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gahirmatha → Olive Ridley

104. Vultures
  • Vultures are important scavengers.
  • They rapidly dispose of animal carcasses.
  • Their decline can disrupt ecosystem sanitation.
105. Diclofenac and Vulture Decline
  • Veterinary use of diclofenac was strongly associated with catastrophic declines in several vulture species.
  • Vultures feeding on treated livestock carcasses were poisoned.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diclofenac → Vulture Decline

106. Pollinators
  • Pollinators include:
  • Bees.
  • Butterflies.
  • Moths.
  • Birds.
  • Bats.
  • They are essential to many wild plants and crops.
107. Keystone Species
  • A keystone species has a disproportionately large ecological effect relative to its abundance.
  • Removing it can cause major ecosystem changes.
108. Flagship Species
  • A flagship species is used to generate public support for conservation.
  • Tigers and elephants are common examples in India.
109. Umbrella Species
  • Protecting an umbrella species requires conservation of a large habitat area.
  • This indirectly protects many other organisms.
110. Indicator Species
  • Indicator species provide information about environmental conditions.
  • Their presence, absence or health can indicate ecosystem quality.
111. Food Chain
  • A food chain shows transfer of energy from one organism to another.
  • It generally begins with producers.
112. Producers
  • Producers such as green plants manufacture food through photosynthesis.
113. Consumers

Consumers include:

  • Herbivores.
  • Carnivores.
  • Omnivores.
114. Decomposers
  • Bacteria and fungi are major decomposers.
  • They recycle nutrients back into ecosystems.
115. Food Web
  • A food web consists of interconnected food chains.
  • Natural ecosystems usually contain complex food webs.
116. Trophic Level
  • Each feeding position in a food chain is called a trophic level.
  • Energy decreases at higher trophic levels.
117. Ecological Pyramid

Ecological pyramids may represent:

  • Numbers.
  • Biomass.
  • Energy.
118. Pyramid of Energy
  • The pyramid of energy is always upright because energy is lost between trophic levels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Energy Pyramid → Always Upright

119. Biomagnification
  • Biomagnification is the increasing concentration of persistent toxic substances at higher trophic levels.
  • Predatory animals may accumulate the highest concentrations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biomagnification → Toxin Concentration ↑ Up Food Chain

120. Bioaccumulation
  • Bioaccumulation is the buildup of a substance within an individual organism over time.
  • Biomagnification refers to increasing concentration across trophic levels.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bioaccumulation ≠ Biomagnification

121. Ecological Succession
  • Ecological succession is gradual change in community composition over time.
  • It can occur after:
  • New habitat formation.
  • Disturbance.
122. Primary Succession
  • Primary succession begins in an area without developed soil.
  • Examples include newly exposed rock surfaces.
123. Secondary Succession
  • Secondary succession occurs where soil remains after disturbance.
  • It is generally faster than primary succession.
124. Ecotone
  • An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems.
  • It may contain species from both adjoining ecosystems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ecotone → Transition Zone Between Ecosystems

125. Edge Species
  • Some species thrive particularly well in ecotones or habitat edges.
  • This contributes to the edge effect.
126. Ecological Restoration
  • Restoration aims to recover degraded ecosystems.
  • It may involve:
  • Native planting.
  • Wetland restoration.
  • Invasive removal.
  • Corridor creation.
  • Fire management.
127. Wildlife Conservation

Wildlife conservation aims to:

  • Maintain viable populations.
  • Protect habitats.
  • Preserve genetic diversity.
  • Reduce human-caused mortality.
  • Maintain ecological processes.
128. Biodiversity Conservation Approaches

Major approaches include:

  • Protected areas.
  • Species recovery.
  • Habitat corridors.
  • Community conservation.
  • Pollution control.
  • Invasive-species management.
  • Sustainable use.
129. Seed Bank
  • Seed banks store seeds under controlled conditions.
  • They conserve plant genetic diversity ex situ.
130. Gene Bank
  • Gene banks preserve genetic material such as:
  • Seeds.
  • Tissues.
  • Cells.
  • DNA.
  • Gametes.
131. Botanical Garden
  • Botanical gardens maintain living collections of plant species.
  • They support research, education and ex-situ conservation.
132. Zoo
  • Zoos maintain animals outside their natural habitats.
  • Conservation-oriented zoos may support captive breeding and education.
133. Captive Breeding
  • Captive breeding involves reproducing threatened species under controlled conditions.
  • Animals may later be reintroduced if suitable habitat exists.
134. Reintroduction
  • Reintroduction means releasing a species into an area where it formerly occurred but disappeared.
135. Translocation
  • Translocation means deliberately moving organisms from one location to another for conservation or management.
136. Biosphere Reserves of High TNPSC Importance

Important examples include:

  • Nilgiri.
  • Nanda Devi.
  • Gulf of Mannar.
  • Sundarbans.
  • Great Nicobar.
  • Pachmarhi.
  • Similipal.
  • Agasthyamalai.
137. Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
  • Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve spans parts of:
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Kerala.
  • Karnataka.
  • It lies in the Western Ghats.
  • It contains forests, sholas and grasslands.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve → TN + Kerala + Karnataka

138. Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve
  • Gulf of Mannar lies along southeastern Tamil Nadu.
  • It contains:
  • Coral reefs.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Islands.
  • Marine fauna.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Gulf of Mannar → Marine Biosphere Reserve → Tamil Nadu

139. Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve
  • Agasthyamalai lies in the southern Western Ghats.
  • It spans parts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
  • It contains rich evergreen forests and high endemism.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Agasthyamalai → Southern Western Ghats

140. Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve
  • Great Nicobar contains tropical island ecosystems.
  • It supports high endemism and coastal biodiversity.
141. Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve
  • Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve lies in West Bengal.
  • It protects mangrove and deltaic ecosystems.
142. Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve
  • Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It contains high Himalayan and alpine ecosystems.
143. Similipal Biosphere Reserve
  • Similipal lies in Odisha.
  • It contains forested plateau and wildlife habitats.
144. Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve
  • Pachmarhi lies in Madhya Pradesh.
  • It represents central Indian forest ecosystems.
145. Important National Park–Species Pairings
  • Gir → Asiatic lion.
  • Kaziranga → One-horned rhinoceros.
  • Hemis → Snow leopard.
  • Dachigam → Hangul.
  • Keoladeo → Waterbirds.
  • Desert National Park → Great Indian Bustard habitat.
  • Sundarbans → Mangrove tiger habitat.
146. Tamil Nadu Wildlife — Overview

Tamil Nadu contains wildlife habitats in:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Dry plains.
  • Wetlands.
  • Mangroves.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Marine ecosystems.
147. Major Tamil Nadu National Parks

Important national parks include:

  • Mudumalai.
  • Mukurthi.
  • Indira Gandhi National Park.
  • Guindy.
  • Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park.
148. Mudumalai National Park
  • Mudumalai lies in the Nilgiris.
  • It forms part of a large connected Western Ghats wildlife landscape.
  • Important fauna include:
  • Tiger.
  • Asian elephant.
  • Gaur.
  • Deer.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Mudumalai → Nilgiris → Tiger + Elephant

149. Mudumalai Landscape Connectivity

Mudumalai connects ecologically with protected areas in adjoining:

  • Karnataka.
  • Kerala.

This creates a major wildlife landscape in the Nilgiri region.

150. Mukurthi National Park
  • Mukurthi lies in the Nilgiri highlands.
  • It protects montane shola-grassland ecosystems.
  • It is strongly associated with Nilgiri tahr habitat.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Mukurthi → Nilgiri Tahr + Shola-Grassland

151. Nilgiri Tahr
  • Nilgiri tahr is endemic to the Western Ghats.
  • It inhabits steep montane grasslands.
  • It is strongly associated with high-elevation southern Western Ghats.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nilgiri Tahr → Western Ghats Endemic

152. Indira Gandhi National Park
  • Indira Gandhi National Park lies in the Anaimalai Hills of Tamil Nadu.
  • It is also associated with the Anamalai Tiger Reserve landscape.
  • It contains:
  • Evergreen forest.
  • Moist deciduous forest.
  • Wildlife-rich hill habitats.
153. Guindy National Park
  • Guindy National Park lies within Chennai.
  • It is one of India's notable urban national parks.
  • It protects tropical dry evergreen and scrub habitats.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Guindy National Park → Chennai

154. Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park
  • Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park lies along the southeastern Tamil Nadu coast.
  • It protects:
  • Coral reefs.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Marine islands.
  • Dugong habitat.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park → Coral + Seagrass + Dugong

155. Dugong
  • Dugong is a marine herbivorous mammal.
  • It feeds mainly on seagrasses.
  • In India, important habitats include the Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dugong → Seagrass

156. Dugong vs Dolphin

Dugong:

  • Marine herbivore.
  • Feeds on seagrass.

Dolphin:

  • Carnivorous cetacean.
  • Feeds mainly on fish and other aquatic animals.
157. Kalakkad-Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai lies in the southern Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu.
  • It contains rich evergreen and moist forests.
  • It is an important tiger and watershed landscape.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

KMTR → Southern Western Ghats

158. Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve
  • Sathyamangalam lies in western Tamil Nadu.
  • It connects the Western and Eastern Ghats landscapes.
  • It is important for:
  • Tiger.
  • Elephant.
  • Gaur.
  • Wildlife movement.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Sathyamangalam → Western–Eastern Ghats Link

159. Mudumalai Tiger Reserve
  • Mudumalai forms part of the Nilgiri landscape.
  • It is an important tiger and elephant habitat.
160. Anamalai Tiger Reserve
  • Anamalai Tiger Reserve lies in the Anaimalai Hills.
  • It contains evergreen, semi-evergreen and deciduous forests.
161. Srivilliputhur-Megamalai Landscape
  • The Srivilliputhur-Megamalai region lies in the southern Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu.
  • It supports elephants, tigers and several endemic species.
  • It forms an important conservation landscape.
162. Grizzled Giant Squirrel
  • The grizzled giant squirrel is associated with parts of southern India.
  • The Srivilliputhur region is especially important for its conservation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Srivilliputhur → Grizzled Giant Squirrel

163. Point Calimere
  • Point Calimere Wildlife and Bird Sanctuary lies on the Tamil Nadu coast.
  • It is associated with:
  • Coastal wetlands.
  • Salt marshes.
  • Migratory birds.
  • Blackbuck.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Point Calimere → Birds + Blackbuck

164. Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary
  • Vedanthangal is one of Tamil Nadu's best-known bird sanctuaries.
  • It lies near Chennai in Chengalpattu district region.
  • It is famous for nesting and migratory waterbirds.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Vedanthangal → Bird Sanctuary

165. Karikili Bird Sanctuary
  • Karikili lies close to Vedanthangal.
  • It is an important wetland bird habitat.
166. Pulicat Lake Biodiversity
  • Pulicat is a brackish lagoon shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
  • It supports large populations of waterbirds.
  • Flamingos are especially associated with the lagoon.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Pulicat → Brackish Lagoon + Flamingos

167. Flamingos
  • Flamingos feed in shallow saline and brackish wetlands.
  • They are associated with coastal lagoons, salt pans and mudflats.
168. Pichavaram Biodiversity
  • Pichavaram mangroves support:
  • Fish.
  • Crabs.
  • Birds.
  • Mangrove vegetation.
  • The mangroves provide important nursery habitat.
169. Muthupet Biodiversity
  • Muthupet mangroves and lagoon systems support coastal birds and fisheries.
  • They are part of the Kaveri delta coastal ecosystem.
170. Gulf of Mannar Biodiversity

The Gulf of Mannar supports:

  • Corals.
  • Seagrasses.
  • Dugongs.
  • Sea turtles.
  • Molluscs.
  • Reef fishes.
  • Marine algae.
171. Seagrass
  • Seagrasses are flowering plants adapted to shallow marine environments.
  • They are not seaweeds.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Seagrass → Flowering Plant

Seaweed → Algae

172. Seagrass Importance

Seagrass beds:

  • Feed dugongs.
  • Serve as fish nurseries.
  • Store blue carbon.
  • Stabilise sediments.
173. Gulf of Mannar Islands
  • The Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park contains a chain of small islands and surrounding marine habitats.
  • Coral reefs and seagrass ecosystems occur around these islands.
174. Olive Ridley in Tamil Nadu
  • Olive Ridley turtles also nest along parts of the Tamil Nadu coast.
  • Coastal lighting, fishing nets and beach disturbance can threaten nesting turtles.
175. Sea Turtle Threats

Important threats include:

  • Fishing bycatch.
  • Plastic pollution.
  • Coastal development.
  • Artificial lighting.
  • Egg collection.
  • Climate-related changes in beaches.
176. Bycatch
  • Bycatch is accidental capture of non-target species during fishing.
  • Sea turtles, dolphins and seabirds may be affected.
177. Turtle Excluder Device
  • Turtle Excluder Devices are designed to allow turtles to escape from certain fishing trawl nets.
  • They reduce accidental turtle mortality.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

TED → Turtle Excluder Device

178. Marine Pollution and Biodiversity

Marine biodiversity is threatened by:

  • Plastic waste.
  • Oil spills.
  • Sewage.
  • Industrial discharge.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Fishing pressure.
179. Plastic Pollution
  • Plastic can:
  • Entangle wildlife.
  • Be ingested.
  • Break down into microplastics.
  • Marine organisms are particularly vulnerable.
180. Microplastics
  • Microplastics are very small plastic particles.
  • They can enter aquatic food webs.
181. Wetlands and Migratory Birds
  • Many Indian wetlands lie along major bird migration routes.
  • Wetlands provide:
  • Feeding.
  • Resting.
  • Breeding habitats.
182. Central Asian Flyway
  • India lies along the Central Asian Flyway used by many migratory birds.
  • Wetland conservation is therefore internationally important.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India → Central Asian Flyway

183. Ramsar Convention
  • The Ramsar Convention is an international treaty focused on wetlands.
  • It was adopted at Ramsar in Iran in 1971.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ramsar Convention → Wetlands → 1971 → Iran

184. Ramsar Site
  • A Ramsar Site is a wetland recognised as internationally important under the Ramsar Convention.
  • The number of Ramsar Sites can change, so current totals should be checked from the latest official list.
185. Wetland Conservation

Wetlands should be protected because they provide:

  • Flood control.
  • Water purification.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Carbon storage.
186. Convention on Biological Diversity
  • The Convention on Biological Diversity is a major international agreement dealing with biodiversity.
  • Its three broad objectives are:
  • Conservation of biodiversity.
  • Sustainable use.
  • Fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

CBD → Conservation + Sustainable Use + Benefit Sharing

187. CITES
  • CITES stands for Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora.
  • It regulates international trade in listed wildlife species and their products.
📌 Must-Memorise

CITES → Wildlife Trade Regulation

188. CMS
  • CMS stands for Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals.
  • It focuses on migratory wildlife requiring international cooperation.
189. World Heritage Natural Sites
  • Some Indian natural areas are recognised internationally for exceptional ecological value.
  • Examples include protected areas in:
  • Western Ghats.
  • Himalayas.
  • Assam.
  • Sundarbans.
190. Biosphere Reserves and UNESCO
  • Some biosphere reserves are part of UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
  • Not every Indian biosphere reserve necessarily has the same international designation status.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian Biosphere Reserve ≠ Automatically UNESCO-Recognised

191. Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

Biodiversity provides ecosystem services such as:

  • Pollination.
  • Pest control.
  • Soil formation.
  • Water purification.
  • Carbon storage.
  • Nutrient cycling.
192. Provisioning Services

Examples include:

  • Food.
  • Timber.
  • Fish.
  • Medicines.
  • Freshwater.
193. Regulating Services

Examples include:

  • Climate regulation.
  • Flood control.
  • Pollination.
  • Water purification.
  • Coastal protection.
194. Supporting Services

Examples include:

  • Soil formation.
  • Nutrient cycling.
  • Primary production.
195. Cultural Services

Examples include:

  • Recreation.
  • Tourism.
  • Spiritual values.
  • Cultural identity.
196. Biodiversity and Agriculture

Wild biodiversity supports agriculture through:

  • Pollination.
  • Pest control.
  • Soil fertility.
  • Crop genetic resources.
197. Crop Wild Relatives
  • Crop wild relatives are wild species genetically related to cultivated crops.
  • They can provide useful genes for:
  • Drought resistance.
  • Pest resistance.
  • Disease resistance.
198. Genetic Erosion
  • Genetic erosion is the loss of genetic diversity within a species.
  • Replacement of diverse traditional crop varieties by a narrow genetic base can contribute.
199. Monoculture and Biodiversity
  • Large monocultures contain relatively low species diversity.
  • They may be more vulnerable to some pests and diseases.
200. Climate Change and Biodiversity

Climate change can alter:

  • Species ranges.
  • Breeding seasons.
  • Migration.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Alpine habitats.
  • Forest composition.

Detailed climate-change facts belong to Chapter 26.

201. Altitudinal Range Shift
  • As temperatures rise, some mountain species may shift toward higher elevations.
  • Species already near mountain tops may have little room to move.
202. Sea-Level Rise and Biodiversity

Sea-level rise threatens:

  • Mangroves.
  • Coastal wetlands.
  • Turtle nesting beaches.
  • Low-lying islands.
203. Forest Corridors and Climate Adaptation
  • Connected habitats allow species to move as climate conditions change.
  • Corridors therefore support both conservation and climate adaptation.
204. Wildlife Census
  • Wildlife populations are estimated using methods such as:
  • Camera traps.
  • Direct sightings.
  • Sign surveys.
  • DNA analysis.
  • Methods vary by species.
205. Camera Trap
  • Camera traps automatically photograph animals passing in front of sensors.
  • They are especially useful for elusive mammals such as tigers and leopards.
206. Radio Telemetry
  • Radio or satellite collars can track wildlife movements.
  • Data help identify:
  • Home ranges.
  • Migration routes.
  • Corridors.
207. eDNA
  • Environmental DNA is genetic material collected from environmental samples such as water or soil.
  • It can help detect species without directly observing them.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

eDNA → Species Detection from Environmental Samples

208. Conservation Genetics
  • Conservation genetics studies genetic variation in threatened populations.
  • Low genetic diversity can reduce adaptability.
209. Small Population Problem

Small isolated populations are vulnerable to:

  • Inbreeding.
  • Genetic drift.
  • Disease.
  • Random disasters.
210. Inbreeding
  • Inbreeding is mating between genetically related individuals.
  • It may increase expression of harmful recessive traits.
211. Biodiversity Conservation in Tamil Nadu

Key conservation landscapes include:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Sathyamangalam.
  • Anaimalai.
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
  • Srivilliputhur-Megamalai.
  • Gulf of Mannar.
  • Pichavaram.
  • Muthupet.
  • Point Calimere.
212. Tamil Nadu Biodiversity Strength

Tamil Nadu contains:

  • Western Ghats endemics.
  • Eastern Ghats dry-forest fauna.
  • Shola ecosystems.
  • Mangroves.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Coastal wetlands.
213. Tamil Nadu High-Yield Species

Important TNPSC species links include:

  • Nilgiri tahr → Western Ghats.
  • Grizzled giant squirrel → Srivilliputhur region.
  • Dugong → Gulf of Mannar/Palk Bay.
  • Blackbuck → Point Calimere.
  • Tiger → Mudumalai/Sathyamangalam/KMTR/Anamalai landscapes.
  • Elephant → Nilgiri and Western Ghats landscapes.
214. Tamil Nadu High-Yield Protected Areas
  • Mudumalai → Nilgiris.
  • Mukurthi → Nilgiri tahr.
  • Guindy → Chennai.
  • Gulf of Mannar → Marine.
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai → Southern Western Ghats.
  • Sathyamangalam → Wildlife corridor.
  • Vedanthangal → Birds.
  • Point Calimere → Birds + Blackbuck.
215. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Endemic → Restricted range.
  • IUCN → Conservation status.
  • Hotspot → Endemism + habitat loss.
  • Sundaland in India → Nicobar.
  • In-situ → Natural habitat.
  • Ex-situ → Outside habitat.
  • Project Tiger → 1973.
  • Project Elephant → 1992.
  • Gir → Asiatic lion.
  • Kaziranga → One-horned rhino.
  • Hemis → Snow leopard.
  • Dachigam → Hangul.
  • Chambal → Gharial.
  • Bhitarkanika → Saltwater crocodile.
  • Gahirmatha → Olive Ridley.
  • Keoladeo → Birds.
  • Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve → TN/Kerala/Karnataka.
  • Mukurthi → Nilgiri tahr.
  • Gulf of Mannar → Dugong.
  • Vedanthangal → Birds.
  • Point Calimere → Blackbuck.
  • Pichavaram → Mangrove.
  • Ramsar → Wetlands.
  • CITES → Wildlife trade.
  • CBD → Biodiversity.
  • TED → Turtle Excluder Device.
216. TNPSC Traps
  • Biodiversity is not only species diversity.
  • Genetic diversity is within a species.
  • Ecosystem diversity refers to different habitat systems.
  • Endemic species are geographically restricted.
  • Native species are not necessarily endemic.
  • Exotic species are not automatically invasive.
  • Hotspot designation requires both endemism and severe habitat loss.
  • India is associated with four global biodiversity hotspots.
  • Nicobar Islands represent the Indian part of Sundaland hotspot.
  • National park and wildlife sanctuary are not identical.
  • Biosphere reserves contain core, buffer and transition zones.
  • Biosphere reserve may include settlements in transition zones.
  • In-situ and ex-situ conservation are different.
  • Project Tiger began in 1973.
  • Project Elephant began in 1992.
  • Gir is famous for Asiatic lion.
  • Kaziranga is famous for one-horned rhinoceros.
  • Dachigam is associated with Hangul.
  • Hemis is associated with snow leopard.
  • Olive Ridley mass nesting is called arribada.
  • Gahirmatha is associated with Olive Ridley turtles.
  • Diclofenac contributed to vulture decline.
  • Energy pyramid is always upright.
  • Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are different.
  • Seagrass is a flowering plant, not seaweed.
  • Dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal.
  • Gulf of Mannar is a major Tamil Nadu marine biodiversity region.
  • Guindy National Park is within Chennai.
  • Mukurthi is associated with Nilgiri tahr.
  • Natural grasslands are not simply wastelands.
  • Ramsar Convention concerns wetlands.
  • CITES regulates international wildlife trade.
  • Protected-area counts can change and should be checked from current official data.
217. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Biodiversity → Genetic-Species-Ecosystem.
  • Endemic → Restricted.
  • Hotspot → Endemism + loss.
  • India hotspots → 4.
  • Sundaland → Nicobar.
  • In-situ → Habitat.
  • Ex-situ → Outside.
  • Biosphere → Core-Buffer-Transition.
  • Tiger → 1973.
  • Elephant → 1992.
  • Gir → Lion.
  • Kaziranga → Rhino.
  • Hemis → Snow leopard.
  • Dachigam → Hangul.
  • Chambal → Gharial.
  • Gahirmatha → Olive Ridley.
  • Nilgiri → Biosphere.
  • Mukurthi → Tahr.
  • Gulf Mannar → Dugong.
  • Vedanthangal → Birds.
  • Point Calimere → Blackbuck.
  • Ramsar → Wetlands.
  • CITES → Trade.
  • CBD → Biodiversity.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is biodiversity? → Variety and variability of living organisms.
  • Three levels of biodiversity? → Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
  • What is genetic diversity? → Variation within a species.
  • What is species diversity? → Variety of species in an area.
  • What is ecosystem diversity? → Variety of ecosystems and habitats.
  • What is flora? → Plant life.
  • What is fauna? → Animal life.
  • What is an endemic species? → Species naturally restricted to a particular geographical area.
  • What is an exotic species? → Species introduced outside its native range.
  • Is every exotic species invasive? → No.
  • Important invasive aquatic plant? → Water hyacinth.
  • Important invasive shrub? → Lantana camara.
  • What is habitat? → Natural place where an organism lives.
  • What is ecological niche? → Functional role of an organism in its ecosystem.
  • IUCN full form? → International Union for Conservation of Nature.
  • What does IUCN Red List assess? → Extinction risk.
  • Does Data Deficient mean a species is safe? → No.
  • What is a biodiversity hotspot? → Region with high endemism and severe habitat loss.
  • How many global biodiversity hotspots include parts of India? → Four.
  • Name them. → Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland.
  • Which Indian islands form part of Sundaland hotspot? → Nicobar Islands.
  • Important Indian coral reef regions? → Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Mannar and Andaman-Nicobar.
  • What is coral bleaching? → Loss or expulsion of symbiotic algae by stressed corals.
  • Major causes of biodiversity loss? → Habitat loss, fragmentation, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change.
  • What is habitat fragmentation? → Breaking continuous habitat into isolated patches.
  • What is a wildlife corridor? → Habitat link allowing wildlife movement between larger habitats.
  • What is in-situ conservation? → Conservation within natural habitat.
  • Examples of in-situ conservation? → National parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves.
  • What is ex-situ conservation? → Conservation outside natural habitat.
  • Examples? → Zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and gene banks.
  • Main difference between national park and sanctuary? → National parks generally have stricter restrictions on human use and rights.
  • What are the three biosphere-reserve zones? → Core, buffer and transition.
  • Which zone has highest protection? → Core.
  • Which zone permits sustainable human activities? → Transition zone.
  • Project Tiger launched in? → 1973.
  • Project Elephant launched in? → 1992.
  • Gir is famous for? → Asiatic lion.
  • Kaziranga is famous for? → Greater one-horned rhinoceros.
  • Hemis National Park is famous for? → Snow leopard.
  • Dachigam is associated with? → Hangul/Kashmir stag.
  • Little Rann of Kachchh is famous for? → Indian wild ass.
  • Desert National Park is associated with? → Great Indian Bustard habitat.
  • National Chambal Sanctuary is famous for? → Gharial and riverine fauna.
  • Bhitarkanika is famous for? → Mangroves and saltwater crocodiles.
  • Olive Ridley mass nesting is called? → Arribada.
  • Gahirmatha is famous for? → Olive Ridley turtles.
  • What caused major Indian vulture declines? → Veterinary diclofenac poisoning.
  • What is a keystone species? → Species with disproportionately large ecological influence.
  • What is an umbrella species? → Species whose habitat protection benefits many other species.
  • What is a flagship species? → Species used to build public support for conservation.
  • What is biomagnification? → Increasing concentration of persistent toxins at higher trophic levels.
  • What is bioaccumulation? → Buildup of a substance within an individual organism.
  • Which ecological pyramid is always upright? → Energy pyramid.
  • What is an ecotone? → Transition zone between two ecosystems.
  • Important Tamil Nadu biosphere reserves? → Nilgiri, Gulf of Mannar and Agasthyamalai.
  • Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve spans which states? → Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.
  • Mukurthi National Park is famous for? → Nilgiri tahr.
  • Nilgiri tahr is endemic to? → Western Ghats.
  • Guindy National Park is located in? → Chennai.
  • Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park protects? → Coral reefs, seagrass and marine fauna.
  • Dugong feeds mainly on? → Seagrass.
  • Important Tamil Nadu tiger landscapes? → Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Anamalai and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
  • Sathyamangalam is geographically important because? → It links Western and Eastern Ghats wildlife landscapes.
  • Srivilliputhur is associated with which species? → Grizzled giant squirrel.
  • Point Calimere is associated with? → Migratory birds and blackbuck.
  • Vedanthangal is famous for? → Waterbirds.
  • Pulicat Lake is famous for? → Brackish-water biodiversity and flamingos.
  • Pichavaram is what type of ecosystem? → Mangrove ecosystem.
  • Muthupet is associated with? → Mangroves of the Kaveri delta coast.
  • Seagrass is plant or algae? → Flowering plant.
  • What is bycatch? → Accidental capture of non-target species during fishing.
  • TED full form? → Turtle Excluder Device.
  • Which major bird migration route passes through India? → Central Asian Flyway.
  • Ramsar Convention is related to? → Wetlands.
  • Ramsar Convention adopted in? → 1971.
  • Ramsar city is in which country? → Iran.
  • CBD's three main objectives? → Conservation, sustainable use and fair benefit sharing.
  • CITES deals with? → International trade in endangered wildlife and plants.
  • Why should protected-area totals be verified from current official data? → New protected areas and designations can change the totals.
